Title: Denial of Service via Unbounded Array Allocation in BloomFilter.readFrom()
Analysis:
### Vulnerability Analysis

A Denial of Service (DoS) vulnerability exists in `com.google.common.hash.BloomFilter.readFrom(InputStream, Funnel)`. The parser reads `dataLength` as a 32-bit signed integer directly from the untrusted binary input stream without validating its size against the remaining bytes in the stream or applying a maximum limit constraint.

Immediately after reading `dataLength`, the method instantiates a `LockFreeBitArray` with the value `LongMath.checkedMultiply(dataLength, 64L)`. The constructor of `LockFreeBitArray` in `BloomFilterStrategies.java` then constructs an `AtomicLongArray` whose size is computed via `Ints.saturatedCast(LongMath.divide(bits, 64, RoundingMode.CEILING))`, which evaluates back to `dataLength` (or `Integer.MAX_VALUE` if it saturated).

As a result, a tiny serialized payload of only 6 bytes (e.g. specifying `strategyOrdinal`, `numHashFunctions`, and a massive `dataLength` like `100,000,000`) will force the JVM to immediately attempt to allocate a huge array (e.g. 100,000,000 `long` elements requiring ~800 MB of heap, or up to `Integer.MAX_VALUE` elements requiring ~17 GB of heap). Because this allocation happens *before* reading any long elements from the stream, it bypasses the standard protection of throwing an `EOFException`.

This leads to an immediate `OutOfMemoryError` or severe GC/heap exhaustion, causing a Denial of Service (DoS) to any application parsing user-provided Bloom filters.

### Conceptual Exploit Payload

An attacker sends a binary payload over a network endpoint that deserializes Bloom filters using `BloomFilter.readFrom`:

```
Byte 0: 0x01 (strategyOrdinal: MURMUR128_MITZ_64)
Byte 1: 0x05 (numHashFunctions: 5)
Bytes 2-5: 0x05 0xF5 0xE1 0x00 (dataLength: 100,000,000 in big-endian 32-bit int)
```

Upon receipt, the JVM executes:
```java
dataLength = din.readInt(); // reads 100,000,000
new LockFreeBitArray(LongMath.checkedMultiply(100000000, 64L)); // allocates new AtomicLongArray(100000000)
```
This triggers an `OutOfMemoryError` and crashes the application/service.
